24 hours with helicopter EMS

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We spend a day (and a night) in the company of the men and women who respond by air to emergency calls around the country.

Unique Selling Point:
Rocket Helicopter Emergency Services owns the largest twin-engine helicopter ambulance fleet in Africa, running a service that responds to emergency medical calls, performs patient hospital transfers, and helps track stolen vehicles around the country. They have offered us full access as their crews respond to duty, day and night, giving an adrenaline-fuelled, behind-the-scenes view of these highly skilled pilots and paramedics at work.

Summary:
Rocket HEMS provides a private service, focusing on those who live in remote areas or work in risky sectors. Today the team might respond to a mine emergency such as the collapse of a dam or shaft; tomorrow it could be a farmer living in the remote Northern Cape, who has suffered a heart attack and knows the nearest ambulance will take many hours to reach him. The company has even been awarded a tender by Polokwane Department of Health to provide emergency services in areas that ambulances cannot reach. Where a helicopter can fly in, stabilise a patient and have him at the hospital within a couple of hours, an ambulance must drive for four hours or more in each direction, dedicating an entire 12 hour shift to one patient, and reducing the chances of survival as the "golden hour" slips swiftly past.
Each helicopter is fully equipped with all the equipment to stabilise and start treating a patient; for hospital transfers, the helicopter becomes a mini ICU that provides everything the patient needs on his journey from one facility to another. Each crew flies with two paramedics - at least one of them with a degree in emergency care. At night, each helicopter must also fly with two pilots, both wearing night vision goggles because they are not rated to fly by radar and must be able to see the ground.
Meanwhile, on the ground, the flight desk coordinates calls coming in and crews going out, responding to each emergency as it arises.
We will speak to the crew members, find out what makes them tick in this high-adrenaline job, follow them on calls an watch as they stabilise and transport patients. We will also speak to the people running the show behind the scenes: the operations managers and flight desk, to understand this complex and high-stakes industry.

Script:


UPSOUND: Craig Coleman: Can you hear me, Claire?
Claire Mawisa: I can…
Craig: When we’re flying, that’s the control – pedals.
Claire Mawisa: Do not touch!

VO1: It’s a hot summer’s day in Joburg, and I’m about to take off from the airfield here at Rand Airport.

USPOUND: Deon de Klerk: [03:58] Medic one is strapped in and secure. Passengers are secure. We are ready to lift.

VO2: We’re spending our day with Rocket Helicopter Emergency Medical Services. It’s a quiet afternoon, so I’ve been invited up in the chopper for a bird’s eye view.

UPSOUND: Craig Coleman: Alright, here we go.

VO3: Next to me is Craig Coleman. He’s been an emergency response pilot for over a decade.

UPSOUND: Craig Coleman: I can’t lie. The fact that you and your crew are in a position to help people in need is pretty special.
Claire Mawisa: [02:13] Ok so tell me what are the unique differences between flying emergency services and normal helicopter flight?
Craig Coleman: [02:25] Emergency services is usually operated at a slightly faster pace. You need to be quite aware of the weather at all times, fuel planning… To make sure that the crews are kept safe. And yourself and the aircraft. We don’t particularly like going out and creating a second emergency from lack of planning.

VO4: In the back seat is paramedic Deon de Klerk.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: [07:54] It’s tight quarters in there, does that make the job more difficult?
Deon de Klerk: [08:00] It has its challenges, Claire. Not only do we have limited space to work but we lose our sense of touch, so we’re unable to feel a pulse, we lose our ears so we’re unable to check air entry.

VO5: Deon and a second paramedic are in charge of the patient all the way to the hospital bed.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: How do patients react? Do they have a sense of what’s going on around them when you’re treating them?
Deon de Klerk: [08:45] Shame, no, we try our best to calm and reassure our patients, if they are conscious, and we have them on headsets because any additional stress can obviously worsen their condition.
Craig Coleman: [12:39] It’s time to strap in, Deon. No warning lights…all good for the landing.

VO6: The privately-funded Rocket crew is on standby 24/7 to respond to medical emergencies around the country. And the helicopter I’ve just hitched a ride in is no ordinary chopper.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: So is this like just an ambulance in the sky?
Deon de Klerk: It's more than that. It's more like an ICU in the sky. And as if an ICU and an ambulance service have married and had babies.

VO7: Deon decided to become a paramedic when he was just 16 and working as a volunteer firefighter.

UPSOUND: Deon de Klerk: One day I was at an accident scene and a helicopter came in with a paramedic and they jumped out. And I thought, no, this was for me.
Claire Mawisa: What would you then say you need to have to be successful at this job?
Deon de Klerk: We are such a mixed bunch. You know, we've got highly academic individuals. We've got some really practical individuals that do this. And I think it's really about the passion at the end of the day.
Claire Mawisa: Listen, two things you haven't mentioned: being able to work well under pressure and not being afraid of heights!
Deon de Klerk: We only function under pressure. You should see me at a pizza shop trying to order a pizza. Without that pressure, I'm a dead loss!

LINK: I’m in the hangar from which Rocket HEMS operates. It’s the largest fleet of twin-engine helicopter ambulances on the continent, and it’s an impressive sight.

UPSOUND: Bjorn Gussenhoven: I think there's well over 6000 flying hours of experience here in terms of HEMS, which is helicopter emergency medical services.

VO8: Björn Gussenhoven is Rocket’s Chief Operations Officer. It’s no standard corporate gig.

UPSOUND: Bjorn Gussenhoven: You are problem solving on another level. Because if we getting called, it's absolutely critical - we're not flying a broken leg. That obviously for us is our passion. We do that well, so we quite chuffed with that.

VO9: In South Africa, vast distances and inaccessible terrain can mean an air ambulance is the only way to reach a patient in time.

UPSOUND: Bjorn Gussenhoven: We've seen areas in the Northern Cape that are not accessible by ambulance anymore because there's complete road infrastructure collapse. You can't get there. So the only way to get there is by air.

VO10: When an ambulance can reach patients by road, it’s at the disadvantage of having to take them to the nearest facility.

UPSOUND: Bjorn Gussenhoven: They technically could spend longer in that hospital to recover because the skill set's not there, or they have to be transferred later. With a helicopter you can do it in a shorter time period, fly almost into another province where that expertise exists and deliver the patient there for the right care.

VO11: At headquarters, the day crew is wrapping up the shift, and the night crew has arrived for handover.

UPSOUND: Deon de Klerk: Here’s the guys! Howzit. You boys ready?
Werner Venter: Yes yes, let’s take it on.
Deon de Klerk: Chopper we’re on is REV. All good, no snags. So we’re good to go.
Riaan [handover on iPad] Right and it’s yours.
Deon de Klerk: Fly safe!

LINK: It’s getting darker, the shift change has happened. Now the crew are doing pre-flight checks. Now we wait to see what the night holds.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: And the wait continues!
Werner- Venter: Yes! Sometimes it gets busy. I've flown from 5:00 and I would get back when the sun rises.
Claire Mawisa: Wow!
Werner Venter: But mostly it is a sitting and a waiting game.

VO12: Werner Venter is one of two pilots on night duty - double the daytime roster. Rocket’s night-duty pilots wear night vision goggles to look out for obstacles, so the more eyes peeled for danger, the better.

UPSOUND: Werner Venter: My work as a pilot is to get my crew there safe and back. Plus the patient, obviously. But my first concern is my crew and the helicopter.
Claire Mawisa: So we’re now killing time together. What do you guys do while we waiting for time? Are we supposed to take a nap or have a coffee? What’s going on now?
Werner Venter: Yeah, We sit around, have coffee, enjoy our colleagues, up to a point where we really going to go to bed and just try to get some shut eye.

VO13: One person who isn’t going to get any shut-eye tonight is flight dispatcher Daniel Kuipers.

UPSOUND: Daniel Kuipers: Give them a few more minutes then I’ll call back and see if we can get some feedback.
Werner Venter: If we can establish the injuries, if they can drive.
Daniel Kuipers: They can’t drive, they’re saying the cars are destroyed.

VO14: Six people have reportedly been injured in a car accident in Mozambique. Daniel and Werner are gaming out a response.

UPSOUND: Werner Venter: I think the best plan would be - depending on the distance - is to get them to Nelspruit. we can offer assistance immediately.

VO15: Seconds later, a call comes through.

UPSOUND: Daniel Kuipers: Ok great. And they’ll take it further from there. Will you keep me updated?

VO16: Stand down: the team won’t be flying this time. But Daniel will spend his night fielding reports like this one.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: Can I join you?
Daniel Kuipers: Most definitely.

VO17: The flight desk is responsible for activating the crew - and for the information they rely on to execute a successful mission.

UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: When the team is out there, do you feel like in some way you are also there?
Daniel Kuipers: Most definitely, yeah. We still receiving information. We keeping all of the hospitals updated. We got to arrange ground services to help. So in a way, we are there. Without us, nothing is going to happen.
Claire Mawisa: So I've actually met the real man in charge tonight.
Daniel Kuipers: There we go.

LINK: There’s an old saying about the life of a soldier being 99% boredom and 1% pure terror. This job is not all that different. While these guys might spend most of their shift waiting around drinking coffee, when the call comes, it’s all systems go.

VO17: Time is always of the essence. An average week involves anything from an inter-hospital transfer…to a domestic emergency…or a pile-up on a national highway. In the week we visited, paramedic Michael Dollenberg helped transfer a two month old infant to a hospital where the baby would receive necessary care for a severe respiratory infection.

UPSOUND: Michael Dollenberg: There was great teamwork between the nursing staff, the doctors and ourselves. It was actually one of our most phenomenal cases.

VO18: This baby was successfully transferred…but not every case ends happily. Handling the family’s expectations is a big part of the job.

UPSOUND: Michael Dollenberg: Being able to bring them in before you sedate a patient, to say, come and give granddad a kiss. Come and say goodbye. If possible, that's something you should be doing. That may be the last time that family member gets to see their loved one alive.

VO19: Dealing with people at their most vulnerable can take a toll on the crew as well.

UPSOUND: Michael Dollenberg: Anybody who thinks that you can come out the other side, shrug it off and carry on for the day is sorely mistaken.

VO20: It’s a challenge everyone deals with differently.

UPSOUND: Werner Venter: When you see some bad stuff, you work through it and you decide whether this is really for you, is it not, and you carry on.

LINK: It’s late, and we’re alone in this big hangar. The crew have gone their separate ways and settled in for the night. We’ve had no call-outs this evening, but there are a few long hours ahead…whatever comes, they’ll be ready and waiting.

PROMO 1 (21 SECONDS)
Deon: [03:44] Medic One. [...] Have you got me?
Craig: Loud and clear. Are you strapped in?
Deon: [03:58] Medic one is strapped in and secure
We spend a day in the lives of the men and women who respond by air to emergency calls around the country.
We never know what we're going to face, so we don't know how sick they're going to be or how badly injured they're going to be.

PROMO 2 (21 SECONDS)
Imagine you live on a farm or a mine in the remote Northern Cape…a medical emergency like a heart attack could be life threatening simply because an ambulance could take the better part of a day to reach you. Enter helicopter medical services.

PROMO 3 (11 SECONDS)
Helicopter emergency medical services are a high-adrenaline, high stakes occupation. We join one team on duty for a day.

TEASER
If you have a car accident in the remote Northern Cape, the only way to reach you might be by air. We bring you a day in the life of Helicopter Emergency Medical Services.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We spend a day (and a night) in the company of the men and women who respond by air to emergency calls around the country.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Rocket Helicopter Emergency Services owns the largest twin-engine helicopter ambulance fleet in Africa, running a service that responds to emergency medical calls, performs patient hospital transfers, and helps track stolen vehicles around the country. They have offered us full access as their crews respond to duty, day and night, giving an adrenaline-fuelled, behind-the-scenes view of these highly skilled pilots and paramedics at work.
metadata.Summary: Rocket HEMS provides a private service, focusing on those who live in remote areas or work in risky sectors. Today the team might respond to a mine emergency such as the collapse of a dam or shaft; tomorrow it could be a farmer living in the remote Northern Cape, who has suffered a heart attack and knows the nearest ambulance will take many hours to reach him. The company has even been awarded a tender by Polokwane Department of Health to provide emergency services in areas that ambulances cannot reach. Where a helicopter can fly in, stabilise a patient and have him at the hospital within a couple of hours, an ambulance must drive for four hours or more in each direction, dedicating an entire 12 hour shift to one patient, and reducing the chances of survival as the "golden hour" slips swiftly past. Each helicopter is fully equipped with all the equipment to stabilise and start treating a patient; for hospital transfers, the helicopter becomes a mini ICU that provides everything the patient needs on his journey from one facility to another. Each crew flies with two paramedics - at least one of them with a degree in emergency care. At night, each helicopter must also fly with two pilots, both wearing night vision goggles because they are not rated to fly by radar and must be able to see the ground. Meanwhile, on the ground, the flight desk coordinates calls coming in and crews going out, responding to each emergency as it arises. We will speak to the crew members, find out what makes them tick in this high-adrenaline job, follow them on calls an watch as they stabilise and transport patients. We will also speak to the people running the show behind the scenes: the operations managers and flight desk, to understand this complex and high-stakes industry.
